key_points: Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Shuffle and Reshuffle" argues that cabinet and chief-ministerial reshuffles, such as Vasant Sathe's removal from the Information and Broadcasting Ministry, are driven by factional accommodation and personality clashes rather than policy.

Bhabani Sen Gupta's "Russia, America and India" reports from Moscow that Soviet officials view South Asia and Southwest Asia as a single strategic region, classify India as an independent "Capitalist" zone held in high esteem, and remain wary of India's economic liberalisation.

An unsigned piece on "Business with China" catalogues the frustrations of foreign businessmen operating in Peking, including arbitrary tariffs of 25 to 300 per cent, housing shortages, and a dual-currency pricing system, illustrated by a rent protest at the Friendship Hotel.

J. G. Tiwari's "Inefficiency of Communism" argues that subordinating economics to totalitarian political control makes communist systems inefficient, citing Soviet private farm plots that supply a disproportionate share of dairy and produce despite covering only 3 per cent of cultivable land.

B. C. Upreti's "Monarchy and the Modernisation of Nepal" traces the Nepalese monarchy from its 1769 founding through the Rana oligarchy to King Mahendra's 1960 abrogation of parliamentary democracy and the party-less Panchayat system, concluding that real economic modernisation has benefited chiefly the rich.

Major M. P. Vora's "The Year of the Child and V.D." criticises the 1979 International Year of the Child for ignoring venereal disease among children, citing a 1920 Bombay Social Hygiene Council report linking VD to a large share of stillbirths, infant deaths, blindness and deafness.

Book reviews cover Lord Denning's "What Next in the Law", reviewed by K. S. Venkateswaran, which recounts the controversy over Denning's remarks on jury composition that led to his retirement, and M. V. Kamath's edited volume "The India of Our Dreams", reviewed by V. B. Karnik, whose contributors uniformly favour expanding freedom over tightening state control.

The Letters page carries S. G. Mampilli's criticism of the October 1982 opposition Peace March for combining anti-nuclear demands with unconditional support for the PLO, and Ms S. S. Rao's objection to editorial language on Farooq Abdullah and Kashmir, to which editor Nissim Ezekiel replies defending the phrasing.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Death of a Dictator" rejects world leaders' eulogies for Leonid Brezhnev, cataloguing his continuation of Stalinist repression, the invasion of Afghanistan, and non-compliance with the Helsinki accords, and criticises Indira Gandhi's praise of his "dedication, tenacity and achievement."

Alexander Solzhenitsyn's Taipei speech, reprinted as "Free China and the Peoples of Asia," praises Taiwan as proof of what China could have achieved without communist rule and condemns the West's and the UN's abandonment of Taiwan to appease Peking.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers Amnesty International reports of rural repression in Guatemala and El Salvador, a Bangladeshi ordinance banning 1,707 drugs, and Milton Friedman's "no free lunch" critique applied to Tamil Nadu's Nutritious Meal Scheme.

Aziz Madni's "Corruption in the Communist Fatherland" surveys endemic Soviet elite corruption drawing on Konstantin Simis's book, describing "Kremlin Canteens," bribery for hospital admission and university entrance, and the diamond-smuggling scandal implicating Brezhnev's daughter Galina.

S. S. Bankeshwar's tribute "H. V. Kamath — a true Karma Yogi" remembers the late parliamentarian as an uncompromising politician who moved through the Forward Bloc, PSP and Janata Party without ever holding ministerial office by choice.

Sandhya Hariharan reviews Manohar Malgaonkar's spy novel "The Bandicoot Run," judging it a disappointment relative to his earlier acclaimed novels despite praising its morally ambivalent central character.

Rama Swarup's "Kabul's Debt To Moscow Requires Piping Out Of Its Gas For 10 Years" details how the Soviet occupation deducts the value of Afghan natural gas exports, priced well below world rates, from Afghanistan's mounting war debt.

A reader's letter from Adam Adil disputes Morarji Desai's claim that Islamic countries are inherently undemocratic, arguing the early Khilafat was elected by democratic consensus and that India's own democratic institutions derive from British rather than Hindu tradition.

In a publisher's note titled "A Fair Deal," M. R. Masani discloses that per-issue costs have risen to Rs. 1.66 against a Rs. 1.25 subscriber price and announces an increase to Rs. 20 a year to keep the journal financially viable.

Nissim Ezekiel's "UNO and UNESCO" argues both bodies apply a double standard, speaking harshly against rights violations by liberal democracies while staying largely silent on graver abuses by communist and dictatorial regimes, and describes UNESCO as infiltrated by Soviet influence.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" defends Justice Tulzapurkar's criticism of judicial activism, hails a Delhi High Court ruling striking down a ban on brand-name drugs, and reports Soviet psychiatric persecution of peace activist Sergei Batovrin.

In an interview conducted by Sumant S. Bankeshwar, veteran socialist S. M. Joshi argues non-alignment has lost its original meaning, credits Dr. Lohia rather than Nehru as its architect, favours a South Asian federation with Ceylon, Burma and Nepal, and urges conceding the Akalis' "just and reasonable" demands in Punjab while rejecting special status for Amritsar.

Rama Swarup's "The Hard Truths Of The Brezhnev Legacy" rejects sympathetic Western obituaries of Brezhnev, citing the 1968 "Brezhnev Doctrine," a decade-long Soviet military buildup, and destabilisation efforts across Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

Minoo Masani's tribute to Vinoba Bhave praises his voluntary fast unto death as an assertion of the "Right to Die with Dignity" and condemns a Bombay High Court petition seeking to force medical intervention as illegal.

Nitin G. Raut's "The Lebanon Massacre" argues that international condemnation of Israel over the Sabra and Chatilla massacres reflects a double standard given comparable atrocities, including Pakistan's 1971 killings in Bangladesh and PLO massacres of Christians in Lebanon.

Shankar Raj reviews M. Chalapathi Rao's "Indian Drama: Traditional Societies in Transition," finding it derivative of Gunnar Myrdal's "Asian Drama" and thin on research despite the author's credentials.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotations page includes the Economist's quip that India is "a functioning anarchy" where "the anarchy is getting the better of the functioning," and Henry Kissinger's remark on the Soviet Union being surrounded by hostile communist states.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Criticising America" distinguishes legitimate criticism of American policy from Soviet-orchestrated anti-American propaganda, arguing a double standard credits socialist states with peace and justice while presuming capitalist ones exploitative.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers an Asian Lawyers' Legal Inquiry Committee finding the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan an act of armed aggression, the Supreme Court's contested 2-1 ruling clearing Bihar Chief Minister Jagannath Mishra in the Patna bank case, and the 15-year sentence given Chinese dissident editor Xu Wenli.

An unsigned report notes that an Amnesty International conference of 120 participants from 30 countries in Amsterdam condemned extrajudicial political killings carried out by or with the complicity of governments worldwide.

Nitin G. Raut's "In the Name of Secularism" attacks a memorandum by 45 Muslim MPs demanding a ban on the RSS and Vishwa Hindu Parishad as itself communal, citing the Minakshipuram conversions and the Jammu and Kashmir Resettlement Act as evidence of selective secularism.

A report on a December 1982 Indian Liberal Group luncheon records LSE economist A. R. Prest's address "Model for Public Finance in a Developing Society," arguing market forces generally outperform government intervention, with M. R. Masani closing by praising Sri Lanka's Jayawardene tax reforms.

A. Kumar's "Food Crisis In Socialist Countries" cites Norman Borlaug and FAO data to argue the USSR, China and Vietnam suffer chronic food deficits from ideological neglect of agriculture, while capitalist producers such as the United States post grain surpluses.

M. R. Masani's "Two Insights" column examines Andropov's KGB background, including his role in the 1956 Hungarian crackdown, and criticises India's refusal to invite Prince Sihanouk's coalition to the March 1983 non-aligned summit as a pro-Soviet tilt.

A reader's letter from Rama Swarup warns that China's test-firing of a submarine-launched missile near Taiwan shows Beijing pursuing big-power nuclear status despite disavowing hegemony, citing the 1979 invasion of Vietnam as precedent for its willingness to use force.

Flora Lewis reviews the underground Soviet satirical novel "The Kangaroo" by Iouz Alechkowski, comparing it to Candide and Orwell's 1984, and Shankar Raj reviews "The Media Crisis: A Continuing Challenge," contrasting defenders and critics of UNESCO's New World Information Order.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "Dead-End Politics" argues the Assam and Punjab crises have reached a point where no short-term solution remains possible, criticises Indira Gandhi for lacking a reconciliatory formula, and warns that separatist demands culminating in Khalistan could fragment India into warring nation-states.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" endorses Peter Bauer's critique of the Brandt Commission's "vicious circle of poverty" thesis, questions the legal reasoning behind Bombay pavement-dwellers' constitutional claims, and surveys Amnesty International's report on torture under Pakistan's martial law regime.

Rama Swarup's piece marking three years of Soviet intervention in Afghanistan documents Soviet forces growing to over 130,000 troops, resistance forces quintupling to over 100,000 fighters, and more than 2.8 million Afghan refugees fleeing to Pakistan and Iran.

Minoo Masani recounts his visit to Taiwan for World Freedom Day, contrasting Taiwan's economic progress with the mainland through comparative income and wage statistics, and criticises President Reagan's "China Card" diplomacy toward Peking as ineffective.

A. Solomon, President of the Maharashtra Rationalist Association, argues in "Science and Moral Values" that ethical values arise from reason applied to social experience rather than religious faith, and that religion has become an obstacle to social progress.

Aziz Madni's "Yes, In the Name of Secularism!" defends the memorandum by 45 Muslim MPs against the RSS and Vishva Hindu Parishad, accusing an earlier Freedom First article by Nitin Raut of tendentious and selective quotation.

Manmohan Choudhuri's "Brutalising the Polity" criticises a Madhya Pradesh ordinance imposing the death penalty for offences like bribery and illicit tree-felling, warning such measures may be used to intimidate the Opposition rather than curb corruption.

Mary Thomas and Thomas George review Maxime Rodinson's "Marxism and the Muslim World," summarising his argument that Marxist practice never escaped the spirit of colonialism and that Islamic sharia is not inherently incompatible with socialist strategy.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial argues the Non-Aligned Movement has no political or moral coherence, since its mostly-dictatorial members condemn the West selectively while excusing each other's abuses, and turns the critique on India's own corruption and dependence on foreign aid.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" contrasts selective outrage over Israel's Kahan Commission findings with the unexamined records of the PLO and Syria, satirises Romanian sycophancy toward Ceausescu, and details Amnesty International findings on torture in Iranian prisons.

An investigative report attributed to the Asiad Virodh Samiti tallies the true cost of the 1982 Delhi Asian Games at Rs. 725.5 crores against an official Rs. 67 crore estimate, documenting exploitation of roughly 125,000 migrant labourers and the felling of 1,342 trees in the Ridge forest.

A translated address by Sun Yun-suan, Premier of the Republic of China, frames the 1980s as a global struggle between democracy and communist tyranny and calls for free nations to reject "peaceful coexistence" with communist states.

Minoo Masani's "From the Sublime to the Ridiculous" pays tribute to the late Arthur Koestler, recalling his charitable fund for Bombay's homeless and his role in the Voluntary Euthanasia Society, before satirising the "myths" of the March 1983 Non-Aligned summit in Delhi.

A reader's letter from Arvind Deshpande of the Trusteeship Foundation criticises the 1983-84 Budget's repeal of Section 35CCA of the Income Tax Act, which had let companies redirect tax liability to rural development trusts.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" covers continued Soviet psychiatric confinement of dissidents such as Petro Grigorenko, proposed BBC External Services cuts, and UNICEF's finding that roughly 40,000 children die daily from malnutrition.

Writing as "Sagittarius," a piece on "Indian Aid to USSR?" argues the Soviet Union, having honoured only 40 per cent of its trade commitments against India's 70 per cent, is effectively receiving short-term aid from India and threatening jobs in export industries like Ludhiana hosiery.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" mourns novelist Constantine FitzGibbon, warns that Vietnamese-backed forces threaten Thailand after Laos and Cambodia, and opposes abolishing octroi while supporting the death sentence in the Joshi-Abhyankar murder case.

Bernard Levin's reprinted essay "Karl Marx: The Tyranny that Feeds on his Name" argues Marx's personal intolerance and the doctrine of the dictatorship of the proletariat gave later dictators, from Lenin to Castro, the intellectual scaffolding for repression.

Mehra Masani reviews "Modern Liberalism," Frits Bolkestein's collection of interviews with European liberal politicians including Minoo Masani, summarising shared liberal commitments to individual freedom, decentralisation and scepticism of both unrestrained laissez-faire and the welfare state.
Nitin G. Raut reviews Lawrence Lader's "Power on the Left: American Radical Movements since 1946," criticising the author's own sympathy for radicalism as a source of bias in the account.

A satirical reader's letter from C. Cardoz, S. S. Bankeshwar, Saby Pinto and P. M. Dias proposes an ironic five-point "formula" mocking the standard face-saving pattern by which the ongoing Bombay textile strike would eventually be withdrawn.

K. S. Venkateswaran's lead article "Are Human Rights Divisible?" argues that India's outrage over a British parliamentary censure motion exposes its own hypocrisy in tolerating rights violations in Assam while selectively condemning abuses in South Africa and Israel.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" argues India is a democratic republic respecting all faiths rather than a secular state, blames Krishna Menon and Nehru for popularising "secular democratic republic," and defends Sir Richard Attenborough's right to premiere Gandhi in South Africa.

Aziz Madni's "The Right To Die" reports on a Bombay seminar on voluntary euthanasia at which M. R. Masani framed the right to die with dignity as on a par with free expression, citing Vinoba Bhave's and Arthur Koestler's deaths.

Homai Jal Moos's "Paraplegia and Society" describes the Society for the Rehabilitation of Paraplegics' work since 1968 and the construction of the "Sharan" rehabilitation centre at Vashi, whose foundation stone Indira Gandhi laid in 1980.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews H. W. R. Wade's "Administrative Law," praising its account of the revival of judicial oversight of executive discretion while regretting it omits comparable Indian Supreme Court decisions such as Maneka Gandhi's Case.

Laszlo Varga recounts the story of Dr. Ferenc Matheovits, a Hungarian judge imprisoned for nineteen and a half years across three terms under Communist rule for his Christian faith, contrasting his fate with rehabilitated Marxists like Janos Kadar.

M. A. Rane of Citizens For Democracy reports resolutions from the organisation's Ahmedabad conference calling for abolition of state Legislative Councils and condemning legislators who vote themselves pensions and housing plots.

Nissim Ezekiel's editorial "The Akali Demands" frames the Akali Dal's Punjab agitation as non-negotiable maximalism, citing its pledge of a 100,000-strong volunteer "army," and calls on the Union Government to act firmly for national unity.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "A Variety of Comment" endorses Peter Bauer's argument that foreign aid fails to relieve poverty, catalogues endemic violence within the Arab world independent of the Arab-Israeli conflict, and reports Soviet arms and funding to destabilise Southern Africa.
A boxed notice announces Nissim Ezekiel's resignation as editor after three years, with K. S. Venkateswaran to succeed him from the August 1983 issue.

An extended extract from Bernard Levin's Times interview with Alexander Solzhenitsyn distinguishes universal suffering from Soviet oppression, criticises Western leaders like Willy Brandt and Olof Palme for weakening resistance to communism, and rejects unilateral nuclear disarmament as moral cowardice.

Minoo Masani's "Two Cheers for the British Electorate" welcomes the Conservative landslide in the June 1983 UK election while deploring the first-past-the-post system's distortion of the SDP-Liberal Alliance's 26 per cent vote share into only 4 per cent of seats.

Anita Gupta's "Freedom for Teachers" argues that excessive rules and oversight have left schoolteachers "paid, but not trusted," calling for the autonomy enjoyed by public-school teachers to be extended more broadly.

Nitin G. Raut reviews John Laffin's "The P.L.O. Connection," recounting an anecdote of Yasser Arafat wringing a chicken's neck and concluding the PLO Covenant explicitly aims at the destruction of Israel rather than genuine national liberation.

K. S. Venkateswaran's editorial "Reform in South Africa" examines proposed constitutional reforms creating a tricameral legislature for Whites, Coloureds and Indians, noting critics call the changes cosmetic since they stop short of local government.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" reflects on the Pope's second visit to Poland and the Solidarity movement, and reports the founding of the International Democratic Union of conservative parties in London, joining Thatcher, Kohl and Chirac.

S. K. Bain's "Soviet Agriculture" documents the USSR's growing grain-import dependence and a decline in output since 1978, attributing the crisis to centralised planning, poor incentives and bureaucratic waste.

Juan Fercsey's "The Frightening Story of the Soviet Secret Police" traces the lineage of the Soviet secret police from Dzerzhinsky's 1917 Cheka through the KGB under Yuri Andropov, noting most of its chiefs were themselves eventually purged.

Rama Swarup's "Continued Soviet Exploitation of Afghanistan" reports the collapse of Afghan tax revenue, Mujahiddin destruction of much of the country's infrastructure, and Soviet extraction of over 95 per cent of Afghan natural gas output.

M. R. Masani reviews Bruce Grant's "Gods and Politicians," disputing its claim that Moscow backed Delhi against China in 1962 and arguing the true parallel to Australia's 1975 dismissal of Gough Whitlam is between Whitlam and Indira Gandhi as populists, not between Governor-General Kerr and Gandhi's imprisonment of Morarji Desai and Jayaprakash Narayan.
Editor K. S. Venkateswaran's "Is Naipaul Guilty?" defends V. S. Naipaul against Indian critics, arguing the hostility toward him stems from envy rather than any factual error in his reporting.

M. R. Masani's "The Isle of Serendip" surveys the 1983 Sinhalese-Tamil violence in Sri Lanka, arguing Tamil Tiger aggression triggered the Sinhalese backlash and defending President Jayewardene against Indian vilification.

Brian Crozier's "How Reagan could start rolling back the Russians" surveys continual Soviet territorial gains since detente and identifies Cabinda, the Seychelles, Grenada and Surinam as low-risk targets for Western-backed rollback.

M. B. Shah's "Secularism: A Dissenting View" rebuts Minoo Masani's claim that secularism is Marxist jargon, arguing it is older than Marxism and conducive to genuine religiousness rather than opposed to it.
Minoo Masani responds to Shah, citing J. P. Narayan, M. V. Kamath and Confucius to reaffirm that "secularism" in Indian usage is anti-religious cant that has bred political hypocrisy.

Ashley J. Tellis reviews Nari Rustomji's "Imperilled Frontiers: India's North Eastern Borderland," crediting its account of tribal unrest as a clash between imposed modernisation and indigenous culture over a Marxist class-conflict explanation.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "U.S. Dilemma In Central America" surveys the Reagan administration's response to Soviet- and Cuban-backed militarisation of Nicaragua under the Sandinistas, citing intelligence reports of Soviet arms shipments.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" condemns the Soviet downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007, criticises the Indian government's use of "deplore" rather than "condemn," and reports on Joshua Nkomo's risky return to Zimbabwe.
Miles Kington's satirical "A Close Shave For Andropov," reprinted from The Times, imagines Yuri Andropov cross-examined in a leaked "trial transcript" to mock Soviet paranoia and propaganda.

Thomas Gay reviews Arun Shourie's "Mrs. Gandhi's Second Reign," praising its rigorous documentation of administrative corruption, misuse of the National Security Act and the Bhagalpur blindings while finding its concluding recommendations comparatively tentative.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews the third edition of H. M. Seervai's "Constitutional Law of India," praising it as a pre-eminent reference while highlighting Seervai's criticism of Justice Bhagwati's expansive reading of Article 14.

A reprint of the 1950 "Manifesto of Freedom," a foundational liberal-anticommunist statement associated with the Congress for Cultural Freedom, holds intellectual freedom to be an inalienable right and warns against emergency restrictions degenerating into permanent tyranny.

S. S. Bankeshwar's letter "A Blueprint For Ruining India" criticises the Mandal Commission Report's caste-based reservations as entrenching rather than dissolving the caste system and rewarding vote-bank politics.

K. S. Venkateswaran's cover editorial "Human Rights in Zimbabwe" condemns Robert Mugabe for re-arresting six white Air Force officers immediately after their acquittal, despite judicial findings that their confessions were extracted through torture.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" argues the Supreme Court underestimated how often hanging fails to kill instantly, and proposes replacing it with pentothal lethal injection, citing the 1982 U.S. execution of Charlie Brooks Jr. as precedent.

Sqn. Ldr. S. K. Bain's "The Lies Behind KAL 007" argues the Soviet shootdown of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 violated ICAO conventions the USSR itself had endorsed after Israel's 1973 downing of a Libyan airliner, and dismisses the Soviet "spy plane" theory as implausible.

S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" surveys Bombay's arts scene, including the Jehangir Art Gallery's Monsoon Show, Alyque Padamsee's lavish production of Evita, and a John Huston film retrospective at the American Center.

Nitin G. Raut's "The NAM Crisis" argues the Non-Aligned Movement applies double standards, condemning the U.S. over Diego Garcia and Israel while soft-pedalling Soviet-backed aggression, and criticises Indira Gandhi's private correspondence with Andropov and Brezhnev.

R. V. Murthy reviews J. S. Mathur's "Industrial Civilisation & Gandhian Economics," clarifying that Gandhi favoured village self-sufficiency and opposed only automation that displaced workers while enriching manufacturers, not machinery as such.
S. I. Clerk reviews B. S. Das's "The Sikkim Saga," an insider account of Sikkim's 1975 merger into India, which calls Indira Gandhi the "main actor" whose "ruthlessness was unmatched."

Minoo Masani's "Rescue, Not Invasion" defends the U.S.-Caribbean intervention in Grenada as a legitimate rescue at the invitation of Governor-General Sir Paul Scoon, criticising the Indian government's vote for a UN resolution condemning the action.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Rule by Ordinance" argues the Constitution's Ordinance-making power has been chronically abused, citing the October 1983 midnight takeover of 13 Bombay textile mills and D. C. Wadhwa's study of Bihar re-promulgating Ordinances for up to 13 years.

Manfred Schonfeld's "Latin America and the Soviet Strategy" argues Moscow's interest in Colombia, Peru and Bolivia is geopolitical destabilisation via drug-fuelled corruption and guerrilla movements rather than economic gain.

M. B. Shah's "The Shunned and the Shunted?" criticises the PUCL's advocacy for Bombay's pavement dwellers as populist overreach, quoting Nani Palkhivala's rebuttal that the Municipal Commissioner is merely performing a statutory duty.

Roger Boyes's "Poland's Prize Predicament," reprinted from The Times, profiles Lech Walesa after his Nobel Peace Prize, noting his decision to donate the prize money to the Church's private-farmers fund as a sign he will wait rather than escalate.

David Davidar reviews Salman Rushdie's "Shame," identifying its thinly veiled real-world referents, including Raza Hyder as General Zia-ul-Haq and Iskander Harappa as Bhutto, and calling it an absorbing political satire.

Govind Talwalkar's cover essay "1984 and the Orwellian Prophecy" traces the books that shaped Orwell's totalitarian imagination and argues that, while 1984 has not literally arrived, the growth of state power and industrial lobbies vindicates his fears.

Minoo Masani's tribute "Freedom Loses Two Champions" memorialises Raymond Aron, recalling his role countering pro-Marxist currents among French intellectuals led by Jean-Paul Sartre, and Leonard Schapiro, the LSE's leading Western analyst of Soviet affairs.

S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" surveys Bombay's arts and theatre scene, including Pearl Padamsee's production of "Children of a Lesser God" and a Gujarati stage adaptation of "Fiddler on the Roof" titled "Dholido."

A book review signed Arun Gandhi covers "The Gandhi Reader," edited by Homer A. Jack, using the occasion to argue that contemporary Hindus who invoke Gandhi to defend cow protection or oppose the abolition of untouchability misread his actual, more expansive views.

The reviewer, recalling his father Manilal's decades of correspondence with Gandhi, quotes Gandhi's chapter on Hinduism describing untouchability as "repugnant to reason and to the instinct of pity or love."

Sumant Bankeshwar's exclusive interview with Karnataka Chief Minister Ramakrishna Hegde has him defending his Janata ministry against Congress(I) defection attempts and the "Moily tape" bribery controversy, framing his politics as a fight for "value-based, clean politics."

A companion interview with Opposition leader Veerappa Moily has him denying the authenticity of the "Moily tape," calling it "nothing but political vendetta," and preferring to contest the issue in the next election rather than in court.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" argues subsequent developments, including a Commonwealth refusal to condemn the action and a Grenadian petition for continued U.S. association, have vindicated his earlier support for the Grenada intervention.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Calling UNESCO's Bluff" defends the Reagan Administration's withdrawal from UNESCO, citing a Heritage Foundation study accusing the body of wasting money and inadvertently aiding "Marxist guerilla-terrorist groups."

A news item reports the Freedom First Foundation's inaugural function, "1984: A Tribute to George Orwell," with Nissim Ezekiel praising Orwell's invention of "Newspeak" and P. G. Mavalankar arguing totalitarianism must be actively resisted.
A reader's letter from Satish J. Shah disputes Masani's Grenada article, citing the 1973 CIA-linked overthrow of Chile's elected government as grounds for scepticism about U.S. motives.
M. B. Shah reviews S. K. Bain's "Afghanistan Will Not Die," describing Soviet economic exploitation of Afghanistan and criticising the Indian government for failing to denounce the invasion.
S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" reviews the NCPA production of Jean Kerr's "Mary Mary" and a chamber-music concert by the New London Wind Trio.
K. S. Venkateswaran's "The Agony of Andrei Sakharov" recounts the Nobel laureate's internal exile in Gorki and escalating KGB harassment of his wife Yelena Bonner following her heart attack.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" praises Governor B. K. Nehru's resistance to New Delhi's attempts to topple the Farooq Abdullah ministry and endorses an Andhra Pradesh High Court ruling that the government's AIR/Doordarshan broadcasting monopoly is unconstitutional.

Aloo Dalal's "Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy And The City of Bombay" profiles the Parsi merchant-philanthropist who founded the J. J. School of Art and J. J. Hospital and treated wealth as a "trust" anticipating Gandhian trusteeship.

West German economics minister Dr. Otto Count Lambsdorff's "Two Views of the World Market" warns against government-directed industrial targeting and protectionism, calling instead for strengthening GATT.
S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" reviews a Bombay production of Shaw's "Saint Joan" and the third "East-West Dance Encounter," pairing Indian classical dancers with Western performers.

Komala Sarathy reviews "The Book of Lech Walesa," and S. I. Clerk reviews "Voices of Emergency," a 280-poem anthology of protest verse from the 1975-77 Emergency, criticising its indiscriminate literary quality.

M. R. Masani, writing as Chairman of the Society for the Right to Die with Dignity, describes the Society's two draft bills to decriminalise attempted suicide and protect physicians assisting voluntary euthanasia.

Vladimir Voinovich's first-person account "Ten Years On" describes his years of harassment and 1974 expulsion from the USSR Union of Writers for refusing to withdraw his 1968 signature defending dissident writers.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" attacks the Union Budget's combination of higher taxation and deficit financing, contrasts it with Margaret Thatcher's low-tax approach, and calls for abolishing LIC's life-insurance monopoly.

Peter Sager's "Nicaragua: The Official Version and the Real Thing" contrasts Sandinista officials' claims of reform and non-alignment with growing militarisation, unheld elections, and a leaked document explicitly describing socialism as a step toward communism.
S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" covers a Rosalind Solomon photography exhibition on Indian festivals and a three-decade retrospective of sculptor Pilloo Pochkhanawala.

Prof. B. P. Adarkar reviews the World Bank's "World Development Report 1983," noting developing-country debt projected to reach $1,997 billion within a decade and criticising the report for ignoring superpower arms spending's distorting effect on the global economy.
Gayatri Jayant reviews Alvin Toffler's "The Third Wave," framing its vision of decentralised, electronic-cottage economies as a modernised "Neo-Gandhism" that will replace Marxism.

Cushrow Irani's "UNESCO and the New World Information Order" argues UNESCO has let itself be used by Soviet-bloc and Third World governments to legitimise press curbs, and welcomes the United States' withdrawal from the body.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "The Tisdall Affair" examines the jailing of Foreign Office clerk Sarah Tisdall for leaking documents on Cruise missile deployment, noting it reignited debate over reforming Britain's Official Secrets Act.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" recounts Arun Shourie's M. N. Roy Memorial Lectures, which used declassified archives to argue the Communist Party of India collaborated with British colonial authorities against the 1942 Quit India movement, corroborated by Masani's own 1954 book on the CPI.
Masani calls E. M. S. Namboodiripad's denial of CPI wartime collusion a "cold-blooded lie" and criticises the Janata Party and PUCL for continuing to associate with Communist parties.

The second and final instalment of Vladimir Voinovich's memoir recounts a 1973-74 disciplinary hearing of the Soviet Writers' Union at which he was denounced and voted for expulsion, describing the moment his "soul" escaped the Union's control.

S. V. Raju reports on a Freedom First Foundation workshop, "How Businessmen Can Enrich Public Life," at which N. A. Palkhivala argued businessmen have obligations to the environment and community while courting politicians rather than the reverse.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Whither Judicial Independence?" examines Justice V. D. Tulzapurkar's warning on frozen judicial salaries and the "committed judiciary" doctrine, and criticises the government's mass transfers of High Court judges.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" criticises Tiny Rowland for pressuring the Observer over its reporting on Zimbabwean violence in Matabeleland, and mocks E. M. S. Namboodiripad's defence of the CPI's 1941 shift from "Imperialist War" to "People's War."

Komala Sarathy reviews Sir John Kerr's autobiography "Matters for Judgement," recounting his 1975 dismissal of PM Gough Whitlam and drawing a comparison to India's pliant presidency during the 1975 Emergency.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews Nani Palkhivala's anthology "We, The People," praising its clarity while noting it omits any explanation of why Palkhivala accepted Mrs Gandhi's brief in her 1975 election appeal.

Short notices cover Khushwant Singh and Raghu Rai's "Delhi: A Portrait," S. V. Desika Char's sourcebook on colonial constitutional history, and Durga Das Basu's textbooks on the Constitution and press law.
S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" surveys Bombay and Pune theatre, including Vijay Tendulkar's "Ghashiram Kotwal" and Bernard Shaw's "Arms and the Man" starring Naseeruddin Shah.

K. S. Venkateswaran's lead essay on parliamentary privilege uses the 1984 Eenadu Case, in which the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council sought to jail editor Ramoji Rao, to argue decades of drift since 1950 have left free speech vulnerable to legislative bodies.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" defends Margaret Thatcher's invitation to South African PM P. W. Botha as less objectionable than Soviet-style "total tyranny," and sides with Daily Express proprietors over editors in a press-freedom dispute involving Arthur Scargill.

Juan Fercsey's "The Grenadian Voice" chronicles the improbable survival of an independent Grenadian newspaper suppressed for two and a half years under Maurice Bishop's regime before resuming publication after the 1983 crisis.
Mary Thomas reviews J. B. H. Wadia's biography "M. N. Roy — The Man," tracing Roy's path from Comintern revolutionary to founder of the Radical Humanist Movement.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews two Indian Law Institute monographs on official secrecy and contempt of court, arguing for narrowing Section 5 of the Official Secrets Act and a statutory public-interest defence.
S. I. Clerk's "Cultural Roundabout" highlights P. L. Deshpande's Marathi adaptation of Brecht's "Threepenny Opera," "Teen Paishacha Tamasha," as the outstanding current Bombay production.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Farooq Abdullah defending himself as a "diwana" rather than a "gadda," and Swaminathan Aiyar comparing Marxist economic forecasting to entrail-reading.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "The Scourge of Torture" reviews Amnesty International's "Torture in the Eighties" report on 98 countries, singling out Zimbabwe's Mugabe government for hypocrisy while noting India's own police are cited for routine custodial brutality.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" condemns press censorship in Punjab following the storming of the Golden Temple and criticises Doordarshan and All India Radio for one-sided coverage compared with foreign outlets.

Conor Cruise O'Brien's "Potent Medicine of the Martyrs" disputes the claim that storming the Golden Temple was a blow against communalism, comparing Sant Bhindranwale's death to Patrick Pearse's 1916 martyrdom and warning it could sanctify Sikh nationalism.

B. P. Adarkar reviews P. T. Bauer's "Reality and Rhetoric," finding it verbose and inconclusive, while Ashley J. Tellis reviews Bauer's "Equality, the Third World and Economic Delusion" admiringly for its demolition of foreign-aid orthodoxy.
M. R. Masani's closing comment on the Bauer symposium sides with Tellis, recalling the Swatantra Party's 1959 manifesto rejecting official foreign aid.
The "With Many Voices" column compiles quotations on Sikkim politics, Ayatollah Khomeini, and Soviet consumer shortages, including an Economist quip on the USSR "rolling itself up like a hedgehog."

In an interview with Sumant Bankeshwar, freedom fighter Achyut Patwardhan disavows his earlier Marxist-influenced convictions, calling himself a "repentant socialist" who was "cheated twice" by the promises of independence and of socialism.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" protests a Congress(I) move to withdraw Goa's common civil code for Muslim women, recalling his own Constituent Assembly advocacy for a uniform civil code, and condemns a new Ordinance shifting the burden of proof in "terrorism-affected" areas.

Govind Talwalkar's "Dangerous Portents" traces the army's repeated deployment to quell civil and communal disorder in Assam, Gujarat, Karnataka and Bhiwandi, warning that reliance on the army erodes democratic legitimacy.
Komala Sarathy's "Delhi Letter" reports a PUCL meeting on censorship at which Soli Sorabjee praised Freedom First and Himmat for resisting censorship during the Emergency.
M. G. Bailur reviews Raymond Aron's "The Imperial Republic," praising its account of America's shift from post-WWI isolationism to postwar global engagement through the Marshall Plan.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews Bernard Levin's collections "Speaking Up" and "Enthusiasms," highlighting Levin's essay on the "seesaw of freedom" contrasting Soviet dissidents with complacent citizens of free countries.
Dr. M. Muralidhara reviews Basil Dmytryshyn's "A History of Russia," noting the difficulty of studying closed societies given scarce authentic information and history's tendency to be rewritten.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "The State of Children" uses a UNICEF report to indict Indian government policy on malnutrition, citing Dr. C. Gopalan's warning that 20 million of 23 million children born in 1983 could be physically or mentally impaired.

Ashley Tellis's "The Politics of Illusion" attacks the anti-nuclear disarmament movement GROUND as naive, arguing deterrence rather than disarmament has preserved the longest peace in European history.

Juan Fercsey's interview "Fidel Tried to Kidnap Me" has Juanita Castro, Fidel Castro's estranged sister, describe him as an opportunist who "created his Marxist history" and warn of a Soviet-Cuban continental strategy extending toward Mexico and the US.

Sharad Bailur reviews Stanley Kochanek's "Interest Groups and Development: Business and Politics in Pakistan," finding its warnings about ordinance-driven governance and concentrated economic power "striking and ominous" for India.
Sharad Bailur also reviews Ved Mehta's reissued "Daddyji/Mamaji," praising its closing chapters on his parents coming to terms with his blindness as the freshest material.
C. G. Pradeep Kumar's "In Brief" column gives capsule notices of five law and politics titles, including A. G. Noorani's edited "Public Law in India" and Roger Scruton's "Kant."
The closing "With Many Voices" column includes a Jaipur police officer's quoted claim that Harijans are "meant to be raped," presented without comment as documentation of official attitudes.

Govind Talwalkar's "Thuggery Checkmated in Andhra" condemns the Congress(I) leadership's role in toppling N. T. Rama Rao's Andhra Pradesh government via Governor Ram Lal and defector N. Bhaskara Rao, who allegedly attempted to kidnap MLAs and branded Rama Rao a CIA agent.

Peter Bauer's "In Office But Not in Power" argues elected conservative leaders like Thatcher and Reagan are constrained by an entrenched anti-market "political nation" of civil servants, academics and media.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" endorses the UN Population Conference's stance against abortion as a birth-control method and cites an estimate of 250,000 female infanticides linked to China's one-child policy.

Komala Sarathy's "Delhi Letter" reports two Punjab-related public meetings in July 1984 at which speakers critical of Sikh extremism, including Lt. Gen. J. S. Aurora, were heckled by predominantly Sikh audiences.

Bhuchung K. Tsering's "The Chinese Overtures to Tibet" marks 25 years of Chinese rule, noting PLA troop strength has grown past 500,000 and surveying renewed contact between Peking and the Dalai Lama's government-in-exile.
An unsigned review of Dr. U. K. Jadhav's "Is Capital Punishment Necessary?" cites statistics that of 105,720 Indian murders between 1954 and 1963, only 1,251 executions were actually carried out.
S. I. Clerk reviews Apa Pant's "The Survival of the Individual," highlighting its argument that consumer society confuses individuals, driving them toward "godmen, drugs, alcohol, sex, violence."

Minoo Masani's editorial "India Has Lost Its Way" condemns both Indira Gandhi's assassination and the anti-Sikh pogrom that followed, criticising the Government of India for selective condemnation of terrorism and All India Radio and Doordarshan for suppressing news of the assassination for six hours.

Masani argues President Zail Singh acted unconstitutionally by installing Rajiv Gandhi as PM without awaiting the Congress Parliamentary Party's choice, following "the Moscow model and not that of Westminster."

Simon Freeman and Barrie Penrose's reprinted Sunday Times piece has Attorney General Sir Michael Havers describe how Britain's constitutional machinery would have smoothly absorbed the shock had the IRA's Brighton bomb killed Thatcher's entire cabinet.
A reprinted South African Beeld editorial, cast as "An Open Letter to Mrs. Thatcher," argues there is no meaningful difference between the IRA, the ANC and the PLO as terrorist organisations.
S. S. Bankeshwar reviews Sarvepalli Gopal's third volume of his Nehru biography, calling it hagiographic and disputing its claim that C. Rajagopalachari supported southern secession.
A short notice on the "Yes, Minister" diaries calls Doordarshan's broadcast of the satire an unlikely bonanza given the network's reputation for governmental servility.
A review of M. Hidayatullah's "Right to Property and the Indian Constitution" praises his historical defence of property rights while criticising his newer, softer stance on the issue.

A review of Ralph Miliband's "Capitalist Democracy in Britain" dismisses his claim that Britain's political system prevents rather than facilitates popular power as a "highly debatable leftist lament."

S. V. Raju's "The Last of the Romans" reviews Rajmohan Gandhi's "The Rajaji Story," recalling how Gandhiji shifted his anointed successor from Rajaji to Nehru by 1941 and tracing Rajaji's founding of the Swatantra Party at age 80.

Minoo Masani's "As I See It" condemns the response to the Bhopal gas disaster, criticising Chief Minister Arjun Singh for touring with Rajiv Gandhi instead of resigning and detailing the swift, unexplained release of Union Carbide's Warren Anderson from custody.

Rama Swarup's "Soviet Union Plagued by Defections" surveys at least twenty Soviet defections in 1984, citing the war in Afghanistan, Russification pressure in Estonia and lack of artistic freedom as leading motives.

M. V. Kamath reviews Sunny Thomas's "Truth Images and Distortions: A View of the Indian Press," faulting the book for devoting nearly half its pages to style guidance rather than substantiating its thesis about a "manipulated press."
K. S. Venkateswaran reviews Peters and Waterman's "In Search of Excellence," questioning how many Indian companies could match the American business culture's orientation toward excellence.

Dr. Thangam Jacob reviews John Nicholson's "Men and Women: How Different Are They," which argues men and women are less different than commonly believed and that "a woman's job" is a social construction.

Minoo Masani's editorial "Give Rajiv a Chance" sets out reform priorities including an economic "U-turn," winding up the Planning Commission, and restoring states' rights, while calling the scale of the Congress landslide an electoral "overkill" from first-past-the-post arithmetic.

Gregory Newell, US Assistant Secretary of State, defends America's withdrawal from UNESCO as a response to two years of policy review finding the body chronically politicised and hostile to press freedom.

Charles Laurence's reprinted report on a Social Affairs Unit study, "Reversing Racism: Lessons from America," argues American racial quotas backfired and that Britain should reject "positive discrimination."
S. V. Raju reviews R. M. Lala's "The Heartbeat of a Trust," on fifty years of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust's role founding TIFR, the Tata Memorial Hospital and TISS.
M. V. Kamath reviews Myron Weiner's edited "India at the Polls, 1980," noting that lower voter turnout correlated with bigger Congress(I) wins.
K. S. Venkateswaran reviews Shakuntala Jagannathan's "Hinduism: An Introduction," praising its glossary as indispensable for foreign readers.
A reader's letter from Satish J. Shah objects to the magazine's earlier uncommented reprint of an open letter equating the ANC with the IRA, arguing South Africa's system is "little short of Nazism."
An editorial note announces Freedom First's conversion from a monthly to a quarterly, introducing a new recurring feature inaugurated by founder Minoo Masani's essay "What Is Liberalism?"

Subramaniam Swamy's "Can Rajiv Deliver the Goods?" questions whether the untested new Prime Minister can govern effectively, warning that his economic and foreign-policy advisers are the same "timid group" his mother relied upon.

Govind Talwalkar's "What About the Software?" argues India's real bottleneck to modernisation is administrative "software," not imported hardware, and proposes satellite-delivered mass training in new techniques.

Minoo Masani's "Freezing the 400" attacks the rushed anti-defection Bill on principled and technical grounds, arguing MPs lose the right of conscience and the Speaker's ruling amounts to a "kangaroo court."

Masani separately addresses the unresolved 1984 Delhi anti-Sikh riots, noting three independent reports concluded the violence was a "politically-sponsored massacre" while the government refused a judicial enquiry.

Rama Swarup's "The Agony of Ethiopia" argues dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam's fixed-price agricultural policy and diversion of resources to war turned drought into famine, with 90 per cent of state investment going to inefficient state farms producing only 6 per cent of grain.

M. V. Kamath's "Ecology—The Drift Towards Disaster" surveys a Worldwatch Institute study on global ecological decline, reporting that West German forest damage from acid rain rose from 8 per cent in 1982 to 50 per cent in 1984, and urges India to expand the Chipko movement.

Minoo Masani's "One Cheer for Rajiv Gandhi" attacks the 1985 Union Budget as continuing decades of wasteful, deficit-financed inflation, and criticises Rajiv Gandhi for backtracking on a reformist AICC(I) economic resolution and abandoning J. R. D. Tata's proposal to regulate migration into Bombay.

Amal Ray's "Erosion of Fiscal Federalism" finds non-statutory transfers have come to dominate over statutory ones between 1951 and 1984, diluting the constitutionally intended role of the Finance Commission relative to the Planning Commission.

Russi M. Lala's "The Road to Dignity" contrasts civic order in Japan with caste-driven resource-grabbing in Bihar, linking a Yadav family's refusal to share well water to a recent mass killing of children attributed to caste conflict.
K. S. Venkateswaran's "The Great Reservation Debate" reports on a seminar tracing reservation policy from the 1932 Poona Pact through a failed 1970 Swatantra Party push to cap reservations by 1980.

The seminar report surveys Subramaniam Swamy's proposed income ceiling and three-generation rule for reservations, and Rajni Iyer's and R. Srinivasan's argument that reservation has become an abused "unemployment guarantee scheme."
The issue's front matter includes a two-part column, "Of Cabbages & Kings," criticising the government's soft handling of Soviet diplomacy around Gorbachev's meetings with Rajiv Gandhi.

S. P. Aiyar's centenary essay "The Indian National Congress—Its Mission and Failures" traces the party from Hume's 1885 founding through Gandhi's mass movement to what he calls "the twilight of federalism" under Indira and Rajiv Gandhi.

Minoo Masani's "What Congress? Which Congress?" personally disavows any continuity between the Congress he served as an underground activist and Constituent Assembly member and the party celebrating its 1985 centenary, arguing it "died when India achieved independence."
A wry piece by Padmini Menon traces shoe- and slipper-throwing as a form of political protest in Indian legislatures back to the 1907 Surat Congress session.

A translated 1886 eyewitness account describes a Coimbatore delegate's journey to the first Indian National Congress convention in Bombay and the hospitality of hosts including Dadabhai Naoroji and Pherozeshah Mehta.

Minoo Masani's "Operation Flood" defends the National Dairy Development Board's dairy programme against press criticism of Dr. V. Kurien, citing the Jha Committee's findings that it benefited small farmers and Scheduled Castes and Tribes.

R. Srinivasan's "Remembering the Emergency" finds most Indian publications, including the left-leaning Economic and Political Weekly, largely silent on the tenth anniversary of the Emergency's end, and cites a survey finding 65 per cent of urban respondents would support its reimposition.
Srinivasan summarises Professor Rajni Kothari's argument that the Emergency exposed enduring beliefs favouring state supremacy over civil society and the suppression of grassroots dissent.
